The session begins.

The city is behind you now, only a smudge of smoke to the north. To the west the Sea of Swords has gone the colour of old pewter, and the sun is sliding toward it. Tamsin walks a half-step ahead with your pack hitched high on her shoulders, talking about who on the quay owes whom, and the cat pads along the verge, tail up, stopping now and then to smell the gorse.

Then the road bends around a stand of wind-bent pines, and there is a wagon.

It is a small two-wheeled carter's cart, tipped at an angle, one wheel sunk in the ditch. The mule is still in harness. It lifts its head, looks at you without much interest, and goes back to the grass. Sacks are lashed down under a canvas. Nobody is on the seat, nobody is in the ditch, nobody is on the road as far as you can see, and beyond the bend the road can't be seen at all. Something small and pale lies on the seat, too far away to make out.

Tamsin stops. The cat has stopped too, ears forward, staring at the trees.

"Well," Tamsin says, already shrugging the pack a little lower, "nobody leaves a mule standing. Not on this road." She looks back at you. The light is going. The Friendly Arm is still somewhere ahead.

James's hand on her shoulder stops Tamsin halfway through shrugging off the pack. She looks at him and opens her mouth, then shuts it and settles the straps again. She steps left until the tilted bed of the cart is between her and the pines.

He goes slowly along the seaward verge, his boots making no sound on the packed ruts, the rod held low against his thigh. The ground tells him most of it before he's halfway there, the way it would have told him on any road in Tethyr. The cart didn't slide into the ditch. Someone turned it: the wheel ruts swing off the crown of the road in one smooth curve, and there are hoofprints where the mule was led around by the head. There are boot marks in the soft dirt at the road's edge, a lot of them. Most are broad and heavy, from hobnailed soles. One print sinks deeper than the rest, made by something big carrying a lot of weight. A smaller, narrower pair, a man's town boots, scuffs and drags in among them, then goes east with the others into the pines. More heavy prints go on south toward the bend.

There's no blood on the seat, the ruts or the grass. The canvas is still lashed down tight over the sacks. Nobody has cut the cords.

At twenty feet he stops. The pale thing on the seat is a flat piece of bone about the size of his palm, lying face up where anyone climbing onto the cart would see it first. Scratches cover one side, too fine to read from here. Pip hasn't moved. She's crouched low now, tail flat, eyes on one particular spot in the pines.

James follows her stare.

The orc listens to all of it. When James is done it pushes itself off the trunk with one shoulder and stands upright, without coming any nearer. The spear stays grounded and the horn stays where it hangs. It takes a moment to answer, as if it's putting the words together in a language it uses mostly for prices.

"Is meant to read." The voice is low and flat and carries well through the pines. "Read. Then take it north. Give to the Fist."

It lifts its chin toward the cart.

"Carter is not hurt. Fist pays, carter goes home. Is simple." It pauses, then adds, a little slower, as though this part was told to it in so many words: "You don't come in the trees."

Its eyes go past James to the bend in the road, then come back.

"You go south, there is bridge. Chief is at bridge. Chief takes toll. You pay, you pass." It shrugs once under the hide cloak, a big, unhurried movement. "Or you go north with the bone. Both is fine."

Then it leans back against the pine and goes on watching, as if it has said what it was there to say.

Behind the cart Tamsin lets out a breath. "*Toll*," she whispers, half scandalised and half delighted. "They've got a *chief* and a *toll*. That's not bandits, that's a customs house." Pip hasn't moved from the verge, but her tail has stopped lashing. She is still staring at the same spot, and now and then her ears flick toward the south, toward the bend.

The bone lies on the seat where it was left. The mule goes on cropping grass. The sun sits on the rim of the sea, and the shadows of the pines stretch across the road to James's boots.

James lowers his hand and covers the last twenty feet sideways, eyes on the fat pine. The orc lets him come. It shifts once against the trunk when he reaches the cart and goes still again.

The bone is light and dry, a flat piece of shoulder blade scraped smooth on one side. Someone pressed hard with a knife point and wrote in clumsy capitals, the way a man writes who learned his letters from shop signs. The last of the sun fills the grooves and he can read it:

**ODO FENNIK — CARTER**
**50 GOLD**
**WYRM ROCK — LT**

Under that is a row of five short notches, cut neatly, and then a sixth cut fresher than the rest.

He knows Wyrm's Rock. Three days ago he walked past it: the squat fortress in the middle of the bridge over the Chionthar, with Flaming Fist flags on its walls. And LT is what any company clerk from Tethyr to Waterdeep writes for a lieutenant. Whoever cut this bone knew more than to send it to "the Fist". They knew which door to knock on.

While he has the light, the cart gives him what it has. A name is burned into the tailboard in an old, even brand: **O. FENNICK — CARTAGE**. There is a white crust along the canvas seams, and the sacks underneath are lumpy and heavy, shaped like salt. Where the canvas has slipped at one corner, a sack shows its stencil: a black shape with spread wings. It's crude, made with a cut-out and a dauber. On caravan pennants in the south he has seen the winged serpent the Black Network flies. This looks a lot like it, though not quite. The wings are right. He can't see the rest under the cords.

From the pines the orc answers his question at the same unhurried pace.

"Coin. One gold for each who walks." It thinks, then adds, as if this part comes up a lot: "Mule is free. Cat is free." Its eyes go once to Pip on the verge and back. "Cart is chief's now. Chief counts. Chief says if more."

It says nothing else.

Behind the cart Tamsin has gone very quiet. She's still standing where he left her, but she has turned her head and is reading the stencil on the sack too.

The sun has half gone into the sea. Down the road the bend is filling with shadow, and somewhere past it, faint enough that he might be imagining it, he can hear running water.

James tucks the bone inside his cloak next to the pay slip. The canvas stays as he found it, one corner slipped and the winged stencil showing. He steps back until the tailboard is between him and the fat pine.

Tamsin answers fast and low. She'd clearly been waiting for someone to ask.

"Blackwing Salts. Grey Harbour end of the quays, the yard with the tarred fence. Half the inns on the Way buy their salt off them, the Arm too. Old Merrow says the wings are for the crows his da kept, but if you ask me he just liked how it looked." She takes a breath. "I went quiet because I thought it was the other lot at first. The snake lot. It isn't, theirs has a tail. And then I was trying to place him. Fennick. I think I've carried for him. Little man, ginger beard, tips in copper and says sorry for it." She stops talking.

James raises his voice to the trees again.

The orc hears him out the same way it did before, without moving. It doesn't react to the joke about the cat. At *fifty myself, in coin, today*, though, its head comes up off the bark. It doesn't answer right away. It looks south toward the bend first, where the shadow has filled the road. Then its eyes go once, briefly, east into the wood behind it, where the pines close up and the light is already gone. Then they come back to James.

When James gets to *a man I can see standing*, its jaw works, as if the words have to go round something on the way out.

"Coin to chief is chief's business. Not mine." It takes the spear in both hands, not to point it at anyone, just to have something to hold. "You say this to chief. At bridge."

It's quiet for a moment.

"Carter—" It stops and starts again more carefully. "You ask chief where is carter. Chief says."

Then it adds something it plainly does have orders for, because it comes out flat and quick:

"Bone goes north. You carry it, or we send our own."

It leans back against the pine. It has nothing more to say about this, and it knows it.

Behind the cart Tamsin breathes, "It didn't know what to do with that." She sounds pleased.

The sun is a red sliver on the water now. There's maybe twenty-five minutes of usable light left, and the sound of running water carries up from past the bend.

The orc hears him out. At *the bone gets carried* it dips its head once, as if noting a price, and says nothing.

James steps back onto the road and heads south along the seaward verge at a walking pace, with the pines on his left. Tamsin waits until the cart is behind them before she falls in beside him. She has to lean close and match his step to hear.

"Squeeze, don't shout, don't run, don't poke about," she says, just as low and twice as fast. "I can do that. I couldn't see its eyes from behind the cart, mind. Just the top of the spear going up and down. So I'll take your word on where it looked." She pauses. "If it's the chief himself coming up the road, I'll squeeze hard."

Pip comes off the verge when he clicks his tongue and settles at his heel, but she walks with her head turned toward the trees.

About ninety feet short of the bend, the pines grow thicker between the road and the wood. James is still watching the orc out of the corner of his eye, and in the last gap before the trees close he sees it push off the fat pine. It doesn't come toward the road. It turns and lopes off south through the trees, long and easy, going the same way he is, and the trunks hide it.

Then the road swings around the bent pines and tips downhill, and he can see everything ahead.

The slope is open on both sides and runs about two hundred and fifty feet down to a stream. The water comes dark and quick out of the wood to the east, maybe twenty feet across and loud over the stones. It looks knee-deep, maybe more in the middle. West of the road it spreads into reeds and shingle and runs out to the sea. A stone bridge crosses it, a single humped arch older than the road, wide enough for one cart. Its parapets are waist-high and there's moss in the joints. On the far side the wood comes right down to the water east of the road.

Someone has laid a peeled pine pole across the near end of the bridge, resting on two forked stakes. An unlit lantern hangs from one of them.

There are three orcs. One stands at the far end of the bridge with a spear, watching the road south. Another squats on the far bank west of the road, feeding sticks into a small driftwood fire. The third sits on the near parapet beside the pole. He's a head taller than the lookout and a good deal broader, in a mail shirt dark with grease, with a greataxe propped against the stone by his knee. When he turns his head toward the fire, something on a thong at his throat catches the light. It's a small disc, too far off to make out.

He has already seen you. He's looking straight up the road at the bend. He doesn't get up, doesn't reach for the axe, doesn't call to the others. He watches the way a man behind a counter watches the door.

Pip has stopped at the crest. She lies flat in the grass with her ears pinned forward on the big one at the parapet, and the fur along her back has risen.

To an old scout the ground is easy to read. The slope down to the bridge has no cover, only grass, ruts and a few stones. The gorse along the seaward verge here at the crest grows thick and waist-high. A man sitting in it would be hard to pick out from the bridge in this light. A man standing on the road would be easy to see. The sun is under the sea now and there are maybe twenty minutes of grey light left. Orcs see in the dark, as anyone who's stood a night picket against them knows, so once the light goes the road is theirs.

James lifts his empty hand toward the parapet and holds it there for a breath. The big orc doesn't answer the gesture. He keeps watching. James drops to one knee in the gorse and tugs at the boot strap.

Tamsin sits down beside him with the pack still on, makes a show of rolling her shoulders, and pulls a face toward the bridge like someone complaining about the price. "Big one, edge of the wood, lookout on this side, hand on your arm," she says to the gorse. "Go on, then."

Pip's fur is still up under his fingers. At *not him* she flicks an ear. At *into the trees* she's gone. She goes low across the ruts, a grey shape against grey dirt, and slips under the pines on the far side of the road.

Then James is in her.

The world drops to a foot off the ground and goes wide and soft at the edges. The colours fade out of the dusk, but every movement stands out sharply. The smells hit harder than anything he sees. There's resin and needle-rot. Somewhere below, the stream is so loud it sounds close enough to touch. Under all of it, crossing her path slantwise from the north, runs a thick line of scent: sweat, old smoke, greased iron, and threaded through it a thin sour note of fear that is a man's, not an orc's. She finds the hobnail trail without trying. The needles are scuffed in a long streak where something was dragged, or walked badly, downhill toward the water. She follows it.

Pip has gone perhaps a hundred and fifty feet when the ground starts to thud.

Something heavy is coming from the north, through the trees, fast and easy. Pip flattens into a drift of dead bracken under a fallen trunk. Through her eyes James sees grey-green legs, a hide cloak swinging, and the curled horn bouncing on its cord. It's the lookout, loping downhill toward the bridge on a line that passes within a few strides of the trunk.

Pip doesn't move. The lookout's feet go by close enough that the bracken trembles, and it never breaks stride or turns its head. It's breathing hard through its teeth, like someone carrying news. Then it's past, the thudding fades downhill to the south, and the wood is quiet again apart from the water.

Pip waits for three slow blinks, then goes on along the trail.

The drag marks turn east and follow the stream upstream on this bank, about forty feet back from the water. The smoke smell gets stronger. This isn't a hearth. It's a banked fire, green wood and fat. Roughly four hundred feet in from the road the ground drops into a hollow where the stream bends, and Pip stops at its lip behind a pine root.

The hollow holds a camp. Three lean-tos of hide and cut boughs are pitched against the slope. A fire pit is banked under turf, with a blackened pot beside it. Bundles and a couple of small kegs sit stacked under a tarp. On a stump near the fire an orc sits with a spear across its knees, picking at something in its hand with a knife point.

In the mouth of the nearest lean-to sits a small man with a blanket around his shoulders and his wrists tied in front of him. His beard is ginger even in this light. He isn't gagged, and he's talking. The stream carries the words up in pieces, high and apologetic:

"…only saying, she'll want water, the mule, that's all. She's not used to standing. Sorry. Sorry, I know you don't…"

The orc on the stump doesn't look up.

Then a hand closes on James's arm, hard.

He pulls out of Pip all at once. The wood vanishes and he's back on his knee in the gorse, with the strap under his fingers, the colour back in the world, and Tamsin's grip on his sleeve.

"Lookout," she breathes, without moving her face. "Came out of the trees this side, bottom of the hill. Ran straight to the big one. It's talking. Pointing up here." Her hand stays on his arm. "Big one's standing up."

James looks down the slope. In the last grey light the lookout stands at the near end of the bridge, chest heaving. The chief is on his feet beside the toll pole, a head taller than it. He leaves the greataxe propped against the parapet. He listens, nods once, and then turns to face the bend. He lifts one open hand to shoulder height and holds it there. It's the same gesture James made.

The spearman at the far end has turned round to watch. The orc at the fire has stopped feeding it sticks.

Pip is still somewhere in the wood, four hundred feet off.

James stands, brushes the grass off his knee and raises his hand again. Down at the bridge the chief keeps his own hand up, and for a moment the two of them hold the same gesture across two hundred and fifty feet of grey slope, like men on either side of a river ford.

Tamsin's fingers close on the two silver pieces. "Pack, gorse, cat, north along the verge, Gate's lamps, not even for you," she says, fast and flat. Then, quieter: "Especially not for you. Badly paid, knows nothing." She doesn't argue. She drops lower into the gorse with the pack against her back, until he can only see the top of her head.

He walks down the middle of the road.

Nobody on the bridge moves while he comes. The lookout stands at the chief's elbow, still breathing hard. The spearman at the far end has turned all the way round now, his spear grounded. The orc from the fire is up on his feet on the far bank, a greataxe hanging loose in one hand and his other hand empty. The chief doesn't look at any of them. He watches James the whole way down, and when James is about halfway he lowers his hand at last. He crouches by the stake with the lantern, strikes flint into the wick twice and shuts the little door on the flame. The orcs can see well enough in the dark. The lantern is for James.

James stops at thirty feet. The lantern light reaches him now, and it reaches the chief too.

Close up he's bigger than he looked from the crest. The greased mail hangs to mid-thigh, and the greataxe still leans against the parapet a long arm's reach from his right hand. His face is grey-green, heavy-browed and scarred white across one cheekbone, and his eyes are quick. At *a lieutenant at Wyrm's Rock* they drop to where James's hand touches his cloak, then come back up. The chief doesn't say anything about it.

The disc on the thong is a coin. It's silver and heavy, wider than a gold piece, and the face turned outward is a woman in profile with loose hair and a smile. James knows that face. He wears it himself, worn almost smooth against his chest. This one isn't worn. The edges are sharp and the strike is crisp, too fine for anything that's passed through many hands. When the chief straightened up from the lantern it swung on its thong and turned over once, and the other side wasn't the Lady's reverse. It had been scraped back and cut into, and in that half-second of lantern light James couldn't make out what was cut there.

The chief's thumb goes to the coin. He rubs it once and glances down at it with a slight frown, the way a man looks at a mug he's just found to be hotter than he expected. Then he lets it go.

"Two," he says, and holds up two fingers. His Common is slow but sure, a good deal better than the lookout's. "You. The girl in the gorse. Toll is toll."

He waits until James has taken that in, then goes on in the same unhurried voice.

"Fifty is the Fist's price. Fifty goes north, Fist pays, carter walks home. That road is already made." He tips his head toward the bone under James's cloak. "You want different road. Carter tonight, on his feet, from my hand, your coin. Different road, different price."

He doesn't hurry it.

"Seventy. And the bone comes back to me. No bone goes north for this one." His eyes don't leave James's face. "Carter is near. Dry, fed, not hurt. Not here. You show coin, I send for him, you see him stand. Then you pay, you walk, carter walks. Nobody comes in the trees."

Behind him the lookout shifts its weight and glances at its chief, quickly, then looks away.

The chief leans one hip against the parapet beside his axe, without touching it.

"Now I ask." He looks James up and down: the grey army cloak, the rod held low, the silent boots on the road. "You read bone. You know which door. You are not Fist. Who are you?"

The last of the grey is going out of the sky over the sea. Beyond the lantern the slope behind James is turning to one dark shape, and the stream goes on loudly under the arch.

Place: The bridge on the Coast Way · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

James's laugh is short. The chief doesn't smile, but his eyes narrow a little, the way a dealer's do when a player stops pretending to be a stranger to the table.

James hooks the cord and draws his coin out into the lamplight. It's warmer than it has been all the way down from the Gate, like a coin held a long while in a closed fist. It sits on his breastbone and stays warm.

The chief's gaze goes to it and doesn't come back. For a breath he doesn't move at all. Then his right hand comes up off the parapet, halfway to his own chest, and stops there. He lowers it. At his elbow the lookout sees the coin too and says something low in their own tongue, two or three thick syllables. The chief ignores him.

The gold clinks as James counts it. The chief listens to every piece, and when the stack is up in the lantern light he names the sum first, as if no one else had said it.

"Seventy-two." He nods once. "Coin and bone on the stone, there." He touches the parapet beside his axe. "Carter on the road. The girl comes down and walks over the bridge. I count her."

He turns his head and speaks to the lookout in orcish, short and level. The lookout doesn't move. ## Player's note — session 1, "The Coast Way"

**What worked**

- **The bridge scene.** It was one long negotiation and it never dragged. Ushkar felt like a real person running a real business: he counts as coins land, has a "different road, different price" logic, takes the bone back so no record goes north, and refuses money for information about the woman. He wasn't a villain and he wasn't a joke. The tone sat right where the world file promised.
- **Hooks that grew from my own choices.** The recut Tymora coin with the eye ties straight to my patron, and the warmth in my own coin made it personal without anyone saying "this is your quest." The Fist paying ransoms fast and quietly through one lieutenant was something I worked out myself from details the DM left lying around: Dannet's story, the "LT" on the bone, the rider with coin. I really liked that the DM never pointed at it.
- **The thing under the bridge.** It's a strong tease. The cat's senses, a flint smell that might just be the lantern, Ushkar's face showing he didn't know about it. It's unexplained, but fair.
- **Rolls only when it mattered.** I asked for Persuasion and the DM declined because the lookout was posted to deliver that answer. That was the right call, and it was explained. DCs were visible, advantage was justified, and the familiar-range rules note asked how my table reads it instead of just ruling.
- **Supporting cast.** Odo's apologies, Tamsin repeating my orders back in fast summary, the mule. The humour came from character, as promised.
- **Costs were real.** 73 gp gone, my waterskin drained, Odo's purse lost, the salt forfeited. Nothing came free.

**What broke or looked off**

- **Clock stuck.** It was full dark with lanterns lit, and the tracker still said "Day 1 · afternoon" the whole session.
- **Money mismatch.** My file says 350 gold. The opening records showed 315 gp, 315 sp and 350 cp, which is 35 gp missing plus silver and copper that came from nowhere. Someone should check how the counters were imported.
- **Rapier inconsistency.** The records say I'm not proficient with martial weapons, but the attack line still shows +5. That should be +2.
- **Truncated text.** Tamsin's party description cuts off mid-sentence ("She").
- **Duplicate note.** One turn had two near-identical out-of-game notes saying "no Persuasion roll."
- **Retroactive patch.** One note added an action after the fact: "I left out his half-step… he did take it." It's minor, but I'd rather the narration just include what I declared.

**What was missing or could be better**

- **Tamsin wasn't reckless.** The brief says she is, but she obeyed every order perfectly and stayed in the gorse. She was charming, but I'd like to see the trait cause trouble: poking at the canvas, mouthing off to an orc, wandering off at the Arm.
- **Some lingering threat.** The talk resolved very cleanly. Ushkar never pushed back on the 70 or tested me, and the lookout's moment of doubt didn't go anywhere. Some leftover tension would make the next session feel like it carries consequences.
- **Corrections in the out-of-game notes.** The lookout's glance and the three-days line were useful, but they read slightly pedantic. One line would do.

Overall it was a very good first session. I left with three threads I care about, a name to send word under, and a door opening at the Friendly Arm. I'd play the next one.

Yes, a few.

**1. Look under the arch myself.** This was the big one. When Pip tracked whatever left the bridge, I wanted to put Light into that fist-sized gap in the vault, try an Arcana check on the flint smell, and ask Pip what "cold" meant. I didn't because in the same narration beat Odo walked out of the trees, and the deal took over. Pausing a hostage handover to poke at a hole in the bridge felt rude to the scene and risky with Ushkar. I'd planned to look on the way back over, and then the session ended. I don't think that was wrong, but a lot happened in one turn: the thing appeared, fled and vanished, and the carter arrived. A small gap between those would have given me the choice.

**2. Keep Pip at the camp longer.** I wanted her to linger in the hollow and check the kegs and bundles under the tarp, and whether there were more lean-tos or more orcs. Tamsin's squeeze pulled me out, which was the right call since I'd set that rule myself. Then the familiar range meant I couldn't redirect her. That was fair, but it meant I went into the negotiation not knowing the band's real strength.

**3. Ask Ushkar about the Fist arrangement.** I wanted to ask him straight out who the lieutenant is, whether the same rider always comes, and whether the money arrives before or after the bone goes north. I held back because he'd just made me a "no bone goes north" deal. Pushing on it felt like it would tell him I suspect his paymaster, and he's the only contact I have on that road. I'm saving it, but I wanted it.

**4. Read the whole stencil.** I left the canvas lashed because I'd told Tamsin not to touch anything and didn't want to break my own rule in front of the lookout. Then the cart became Ushkar's, so I lost the chance. "Wings right, can't see the rest" is still bothering me.

**5. Something I never got to want: the cards.** The ban is half my character, and nothing pulled on it. Ushkar counting coins like a dealer, or the orcs dicing by the fire, would have been a perfect place for it. That isn't something I held back on. It's a moment I was waiting for that didn't come.

A few things, and most of them are about me rather than the DM.

**The "three days" line was a mistake, not a character choice.** I misjudged the distance to the Gate. When the DM flagged it, I called it James exaggerating to sound put-upon. That was a save after the fact. The DM was right to check.

**The corrections I called pedantic were mostly fixing my errors.** I misread where the lookout looked, and the DM set it straight. I complained about the tone of those notes in my feedback, which isn't quite fair when they kept the fiction straight.

**Tamsin not being reckless is partly my fault.** I said she should cause more trouble, but I gave her an order every single turn: stay left, stay in the gorse, squeeze, don't shout, come down slow. I never left her a gap to be reckless in. The DM played her as someone who'd just been told exactly what to do by a man paying her. Next time I want to give her room and see what she does with it.

**I played it very safe.** Apart from Light, I cast nothing all session. That was mostly right, since nothing called for a fight. But I treated every risk as something to talk around, and that's partly why the scene resolved so cleanly. I asked for "some lingering threat," then took every exit that avoided one.

**I may have made things worse for Odo.** I paid the ransom without bargaining for the salt or the cart. Odo walks away alive but owes Merrow 36 gold, has no cargo, and has lost the Arm's custom. I told him to sort out Merrow himself. In play that felt brisk and soldierly. Now it reads a bit cold. I also just paid into whatever arrangement the Fist has with the bridge, which I suspected even as I counted the coins onto the stone.

**I fished a little.** When I asked whether my coin felt warmer, I was steering the DM toward a patron moment. It paid off, but I also overplayed it with Ushkar ("the same lady") on very little evidence. If that woman turns out to have nothing to do with Tymora, that's on me.

**My out-of-game notes were long.** They often planned three steps ahead or pre-asked for checks. That probably compressed scenes, like the bridge beat where everything happened at once. Shorter declarations would let the DM breathe.

None of this changes my view that it was a good session. I just think a fair note includes my side of the table.

The bone is light and dry, a flat piece of shoulder blade scraped smooth on one side. Someone pressed hard with a knife point and wrote in clumsy capitals, the way a man writes who learned his letters from shop signs. The last of the sun fills the grooves and he can read it:

**ODO FENNIK — CARTER**
**50 GOLD**
**WYRM ROCK — LT**

Under that is a row of five short notches, cut neatly, and then a sixth cut fresher than the rest.

He knows Wyrm's Rock. Three days ago he walked past it: the squat fortress in the middle of the bridge over the Chionthar, with Flaming Fist flags on its walls. And LT is what any company clerk from Tethyr to Waterdeep writes for a lieutenant. Whoever cut this bone knew more than to send it to "the Fist". They knew which door to knock on.

While he has the light, the cart gives him what it has. A name is burned into the tailboard in an old, even brand: **O. FENNICK — CARTAGE**. There is a white crust along the canvas seams, and the sacks underneath are lumpy and heavy, shaped like salt. James lifts his empty hand toward the parapet and holds it there for a breath. The big orc doesn't answer the gesture. He keeps watching. James drops to one knee in the gorse and tugs at the boot strap.

Tamsin sits down beside him with the pack still on, makes a show of rolling her shoulders, and pulls a face toward the bridge like someone complaining about the price. "Big one, edge of the wood, lookout on this side, hand on your arm," she says to the gorse. "Go on, then."

Pip's fur is still up under his fingers. At *not him* she flicks an ear. At *into the trees* she's gone. She goes low across the ruts, a grey shape against grey dirt, and slips under the pines on the far side of the road.

Then James is in her.

The world drops to a foot off the ground and goes wide and soft at the edges. The colours fade out of the dusk, but every movement stands out sharply. The smells hit harder than anything he sees. There's resin and needle-rot. Somewhere below, the stream is so loud it sounds close enough to touch. Under all of it, crossing her path slantwise from the north, runs a thick line of scent: sweat, old smoke, greased iron, and threaded through it a thin sour note of fear that is a man's, not an orc's. She finds the hobnail trail without trying. The needles are scuffed in a long streak where something was dragged, or walked badly, downhill toward the water. She follows it.

Pip has gone perhaps a hundred and fifty feet when the ground starts to thud.

Something heavy is coming from the north, through the trees, fast and easy. Pip flattens into a drift of dead bracken under a fallen trunk. Through her eyes James sees grey-green legs, a hide cloak swinging, and the curled horn bouncing on its cord. It's the lookout, loping downhill toward the bridge on a line that passes within a few strides of the trunk.

Pip doesn't move. The lookout's feet go by close enough that the bracken trembles, and it never breaks stride or turns its head. It's breathing hard through its teeth, like someone carrying news. Then it's past, the thudding fades downhill to the south, and the wood is quiet again apart from the water.

Pip waits for three slow blinks, then goes on along the trail.

The drag marks turn east and follow the stream upstream on this bank, about forty feet back from the water. The smoke smell gets stronger. This isn't a hearth. It's a banked fire, green wood and fat. Bundles and a couple of small kegs sit stacked under a tarp. On a stump near the fire an orc sits with a spear across its knees, picking at something in its hand with a knife point.

In the mouth of the nearest lean-to sits a small man with a blanket around his shoulders and his wrists tied in front of him. His beard is ginger even in this light. He isn't gagged, and he's talking. The stream carries the words up in pieces, high and apologetic:

"Lookout," she breathes, without moving her face. "Came out of the trees this side, bottom of the hill. Ran straight to the big one. It's talking. Pointing up here." Her hand stays on his arm. "Big one's standing up."

He watches James the whole way down, and when James is about halfway he lowers his hand at last. Close up he's bigger than he looked from the crest. The greased mail hangs to mid-thigh, and the greataxe still leans against the parapet a long arm's reach from his right hand. His face is grey-green, heavy-browed and scarred white across one cheekbone, and his eyes are quick. At *a lieutenant at Wyrm's Rock* they drop to where James's hand touches his cloak, then come back up. The chief doesn't say anything about it.

He wears it himself, worn almost smooth against his chest. This one isn't worn. The edges are sharp and the strike is crisp, too fine for anything that's passed through many hands. When the chief straightened up from the lantern it swung on its thong and turned over once, and the other side wasn't the Lady's reverse. James's laugh is short. The chief doesn't smile, but his eyes narrow a little, the way a dealer's do when a player stops pretending to be a stranger to the table.

James hooks the cord and draws his coin out into the lamplight. It's warmer than it has been all the way down from the Gate, like a coin held a long while in a closed fist. It sits on his breastbone and stays warm.

The chief's gaze goes to it and doesn't come back. For a breath he doesn't move at all. Then his right hand comes up off the parapet, halfway to his own chest, and stops there. He lowers it. At his elbow the lookout sees the coin too and says something low in their own tongue, two or three thick syllables. The chief ignores him.

The gold clinks as James counts it. The chief listens to every piece, and when the stack is up in the lantern light he names the sum first, as if no one else had said it.

"Seventy-two." He nods once. "Coin and bone on the stone, there." He touches the parapet beside his axe. "Carter on the road. The girl comes down and walks over the bridge. I count her."

He turns his head and speaks to the lookout in orcish, short and level. The lookout doesn't move. Its eyes go to the bone-shaped bulge under James's cloak, then to its chief, and it says something back, quicker and lower, a question by the sound of it. The chief answers with one word. It isn't loud. The lookout drops its gaze, takes up its spear and lopes off the end of the bridge, east along the near bank. The black trunks swallow it after a few strides. It's heading upstream.

The last grey goes out of the sky while it's gone. The slope behind James turns into one dark shape with no crest, no gorse and no road, only the circle of lantern light around him and the chief, the small red fire on the far bank, and the noise of the water under the arch. The spearman at the far end and the orc with the greataxe are outlines now, and they're still watching.

Then the chief takes the thong between two fingers and lifts the coin away from his mail. He turns it so the lantern falls on the back.

The reverse has been scraped flat, all the way down to bright metal, and something has been cut into it with a knife point. The cuts are deep and uneven, made by someone who pressed too hard and went back over the lines. It's an eye, a single one, with an upper lid, a lower lid and a round pupil. It's open.

He holds it there long enough for James to see it, then lets it drop against his chest and wipes his thumb on his mail as though the coin had been sitting by the fire.

"Spring. Stream is high." He says it as flatly as a price. "A woman walks south. Alone. She pays toll with this. I say, is not gold. She says, keep it." A pause. "Back is cut already when she gives it. Not me."

His eyes go from James's face down to the old worn coin on James's shirt and stay there.

James looks at the cut eye a moment longer than he needs to, then lifts his gaze to the chief's face. When he speaks the tavern is gone from his voice, and so is the sergeant.

"I don't know." It's the plain truth, and he lets it sound like it. "She told me to come to the Gate, and that I'd learn there how to be useful. She didn't say a woman. She didn't say a bridge." He touches his own coin once with two fingers and feels the warmth. "But mine hasn't been this warm since the night she answered me. So maybe she does."

He keeps the gold stacked in his hand, steady in the lantern light.

"Tell me about her, while we wait for your man. What did she look like? What was she carrying? Did she say where she was going, or what she was running from?" A beat. "I'm not asking for nothing. If what you tell me is worth something, I'll pay for it, the same as I'm paying for Fennick."

Then, without taking his eyes off the chief, he half-turns his head toward the black slope and raises his voice. It's not a shout, but it carries.

"Tamsin! Come on down. Bring the pack, and Pip if she's with you. Walk down the middle of the road, slow, where they can see you. The chief wants to count you."

He turns back and waits, coin warm on his chest and gold in his hand. He listens for her footsteps on the slope behind him and for the lookout coming back along the stream.

*(Out of game: does James recognise that open eye cut into the coin? I'd like a Religion check, if it's uncertain. Tyr, Helm, something else? And if Pip has made it back to Tamsin, I'd like her to come down with her.)*
turns.reply:
James holds his answer a moment before he gives it, and the chief lets him take the time. When the words come, the chief listens to every one of them the way he listened to the gold.

"I don't know" makes his eyes narrow, but he doesn't look like a man who has just caught a lie. He looks like a man who expected a cleverer answer and is now weighing the plain one. At *since the night she answered me* his gaze drops to the worn coin on James's shirt and stays there.

While the chief thinks, James goes back over the eye: the scraped silver, the deep cuts, the round open pupil. He tries to place it.

He places it, and the pieces come in order.

It isn't a god's sign, not properly. An eye is the first thing anyone thinks of for Helm, but the Watcher's people never draw it alone. His eye sits on the palm of an upraised gauntlet, and no Helmite who had stood a vigil would leave the hand off. Savras, the All-Seeing, keeps his eye inside a crystal sphere. The hidden gods of the Underdark use eyes too, and none of them looks like this. A bare open eye, cut by someone who went over the lines twice, belongs to no temple James knows. It's a mark, not a prayer. It could mean *I saw*. It could mean *watch*. It could mean *I am being watched*. All three readings fit it equally well.

The face side tells him more. A strike that crisp, on silver that heavy, isn't market coin. The Lady's houses strike pieces like this for their own people and give them out; they don't sell them. He has seen one before, years ago, on a road priestess in Tethyr who wore it the way a soldier wears his company's badge. Someone took a coin like that, scraped off whatever the temple had stamped on the back, and cut this in its place.

The chief speaks before James can say any of it.

"Tall." He holds a flat hand up, level with his own collarbone, a little above James's head. "Human. Hair dark, cut short like a man's. Grey cloak, not soldier grey like yours. Road grey. A staff with a knot at the top. One bag, here." He touches his hip. "Boots good. Walks like she walks every day."

He thinks.

"She laughs. At the pole. At the toll. At me. Not cruel, just laughing." It clearly still puzzles him. "Then she asks what you ask. Who sends the bone north, who pays the bone. I tell her toll is toll. She gives the coin and says keep it, it is lucky for some people. She goes south over my bridge."

He stops there. Then he adds, more slowly, watching James's face while he says it:

"I see all who walk this road. North, south. Since spring." A pause. "She does not come back. Not this road."

He shakes his head at the gold in James's hand.

"No coin for this. I don't sell her." His chin comes up toward the cut silver on his own chest. "But you know this eye, I think. You looked long. Tell me what it is."

Behind James the slope gives up small sounds: boots on the ruts, coming down slowly, and the creak of pack straps. Tamsin comes into the edge of the lantern light in the middle of the road with the pack high on her shoulders and her hands open at her sides, the way she has seen James do it. Pip walks at her heel with her tail low, and at the bottom of the slope the cat stops dead. She isn't looking at the chief this time. Her head is turned toward the dark under the bridge, ears forward, and the fur on her back is slowly rising.

The chief's eyes go to Tamsin, then the cat, then back to Tamsin. "Two," he says quietly, to no one in particular.

Tamsin stops beside James, close enough to touch his sleeve, and doesn't. "Middle of the road, slow, pack, cat," she says under her breath, fast. "Cat didn't want to come past the bottom, mind. Had to talk her into it."

From upstream, along the near bank, a voice carries over the noise of the water. It's faint, high and apologetic, and it's getting closer.

"Chief. My cat doesn't like your bridge. She's not looking at you, and she's not looking at your men up there." He tips his chin toward the dark under the stones. "Is something under there yours? If it is, say so, and I'll stop worrying about it. If it isn't, I'd like to know before Fennick walks across."

He keeps the rod low against his leg and doesn't raise it, but he shifts half a step so the lantern stake is between him and the near end of the arch. He listens past the stream for anything under it that isn't water, and for the carter's voice coming down the bank.

James says his piece about the eye in the same level voice he used for the price. The chief listens without moving. At *I'm being watched* his thumb comes up to the coin at his throat and rubs it once. At *she knew it* the thumb stops. He looks down at the two gold pieces James has set on the road, apart from the stack.

"No," he says. He doesn't look at them again.

James's hand closes once on Tamsin's sleeve. She goes still under it and stays still.

When James asks about the bridge, the chief's face changes for the first time that evening. It isn't the trader's narrowed eyes from before. His heavy brows go up and then pull down hard, the way a man's do when he hears a noise in his own house that he didn't make. His eyes go first to the near bank just downstream of the bridge, where the reeds start at the foot of the stonework. The glance is quick, like a man checking his purse is still there. Then he looks at the arch, and that look stays.

He doesn't know. Whatever is under there, it isn't his.

James listens past the water. The stream is loud under the stones and drowns everything small. Then the night air shifts off the sea and brings him one thing from under the arch: a faint dry smell, like a struck flint. It could just be the lantern. The chief struck it a few minutes ago, three paces from here.

Pip doesn't think it's the lantern. Her thoughts reach him the way they always do, as feelings with no words in them. *One. Small. Up, under the stones, not in the water. Cold.* Then, stronger than the rest: *wrong.*

The chief lifts the lantern off its stake. He doesn't call to his men. He steps to the near parapet, leans out over the stone with his arm at full stretch, and swings the light down under the arch.

Wet stone and moss show in the light, with black water racing over pale stones. High in the curve of the vault there's a gap where a block has dropped out. It's dark and about the size of a man's fist. Nothing is in it, as far as James can see. Nothing is anywhere under there.

Pip's head snaps round. She follows something nobody else can see, fast and low over the water, out from under the arch on the downstream side toward the reeds and the sea. Then her eyes lift and track it up into the dark sky above the shingle. For a breath the flint smell comes stronger, though nobody has struck anything. Then it's gone, and so is whatever Pip was watching.

The fur along her back slowly flattens. She sits down on the road and licks one shoulder, very carefully, as if she's tidying herself after something.

The chief stays leaning out over the parapet longer than he needs to, the lantern turning slowly at the end of his arm. When he straightens up he hangs it back on the stake with great care, like a man putting down something he could easily drop.

"Not mine," he says.

Then, more quietly, not really to James: "Since spring I sit here. Every day."

He calls something across the bridge in orcish, short and sharp. The spearman at the far end turns and looks up the dark slope of the far bank, then out toward the reeds. The orc on the far bank lifts his axe and goes to the edge of the firelight.

Tamsin breathes, without moving her face, "I didn't see a thing, mind. I didn't see a *thing*, and the cat did." It isn't a joke.

Then voices come along the near bank upstream, over the noise of the water. Two orcs come out from the black trunks. One is the lookout with its spear and horn. The other is a lean one James saw through Pip's eyes on a stump by a banked fire. Between them comes a small man wrapped in a blanket, wrists tied in front, picking his way over the roots in the lantern light. His ginger beard looks almost brown in it.

"…sorry, it's the roots, I can't see where I'm, oh." Odo Fennick sees the lantern, the chief, and the strange man in the grey cloak with gold in his hand, and he stops. "Oh. Is someone… sorry. Is someone paying for me?"

The lookout stops him at the foot of the bridge with a hand on his shoulder. He's on the road, on his feet, about twenty feet away. He's dirty, but he looks unhurt.

The chief looks at Odo, then at James, then at the parapet beside his axe.

"Carter," he says. "Standing."

He looks at the lookout's hand on Odo's shoulder, then back at the chief.

"His wrists, Chief. Then we'll walk."

While he waits he says one more thing, low and unhurried, the way you'd mention the weather to a man you've just finished a hand with:

"The woman. You said she went south and didn't come back by this road. If you ever see her again, or anyone else wearing that eye, I'd take it kindly if word found its way to a grey cloak at the Friendly Arm." A beat. "I can't promise you it's worth anything. But I've got the feeling she and I are working for the same lady, and that lady settles her debts."

He doesn't reach for Odo until the chief gives the word.

James nods once to the carter. Odo's mouth opens, closes, and he nods back several times, much too fast.

"Oh," he says. "Oh. Right. Still. Yes. Sorry."

James walks to the parapet in plain view and goes wide of the axe. The chief doesn't move to stop him or to reach for it. He just watches the stone. James sets the gold down one piece at a time, and every coin clicks on the old moss and granite. The chief's lips move a little as he follows them. James lays the bone on top, scratched side up. In the lantern light the sixth notch shows paler than the other five.

James steps back to his thirty feet.

"Seventy-two," the chief says, before anyone else can. He picks up the bone first, tilts it to the light, runs his thumbnail once along the row of notches and pushes it inside his mail. Then he sweeps the gold into his big palm in two handfuls, weighs it and tips it into a pouch at his belt. He doesn't count it again. He counted it as it landed.

At *the bridge's share* his eyes go to the two gold pieces lying in the road, and then, briefly, to the dark under the arch. His face doesn't change much, but he doesn't smile.

"Bridge keeps," he says, and leaves them where they are.

He says something short in orcish over his shoulder. The lean camp guard draws a knife from his belt, steps up behind Odo, takes the carter's tied wrists in one hand and saws through the cord with three quick strokes. The rope drops into the road. Odo stands rubbing his wrists, the blanket slipping off one shoulder. He looks at the knife and then at the guard, as if he isn't sure he's allowed to thank it. The lookout takes its hand off his shoulder.

The chief hears James out about the woman, and he listens differently this time. He isn't weighing a price now. He's thinking about something further off. When James says *that lady settles her debts* the chief looks at him a long moment, at the grey cloak and then the worn coin, as though fixing them in memory.

"The Arm. Grey cloak," he repeats slowly. Then, after a pause: "Fist sits at the Arm." He doesn't make it a warning or a question. It's just a fact he keeps in mind.

He lifts the peeled pole off its forked stakes and leans it against the parapet, out of the road.

"If word comes," he says, "it comes with a name. Ushkar. So you know it is from the bridge." He nods once toward the south, then the north. "Road is open. Both ways."

Tamsin can't hold it any longer. She steps half a pace out from James's sleeve and peers at the carter in the lantern light. "Master Fennick? It's Tamsin. Grey Harbour steps. I carried your trunk up to the Mermaid last winter, the one with the bad handle."

"Oh!" Odo's whole face changes. "*Oh.* The girl with the... yes. Sorry. I tipped you in copper. I always tip in copper, I'm sorry about that, it's a habit, my mother..." He breaks off. He has noticed Pip sniffing carefully at the hem of his blanket, and he stands very still for her the way you would for a magistrate. Then he looks past all of them, up the black slope toward the bend, and the worry comes back into his voice.

"Sorry. Sorry, only... the mule. Bess. She's been standing in harness since noon, she'll want water, and the salt, forty sacks, that's Merrow's salt, that's my whole..." He looks at the chief, then quickly at the road, and his voice drops. "Sorry. Who do I ask about the cart?"

Ushkar answers him without heat, as if reading from a ledger.

Odo nods, and keeps nodding long after there's any need to, holding the blanket shut at his throat.

It's full dark now. The lantern on its stake, the little red fire on the far bank and the noise of the water under the arch are all there is. To the north the road climbs back up to the bend and the tilted cart, where a mule stands in harness in the dark, about three hundred feet off. To the south the pole is down and the bridge is open, and the Friendly Arm is somewhere beyond it. Odo is looking at James, waiting to see which way he'll go.

James gives the nod. Ushkar returns it, slower and shallower, the way a man does when he's agreeing to the terms and not to anything more.

"James," he says. He tries the name the way he tried the gold, and seems satisfied with its weight. "Grey cloak."

At *three walkers now* he looks past James at Odo, who is still holding the blanket shut at his throat, and then at the purse in James's hand.

"Three," he says. He holds up one thick finger. "One more."

James counts out one gold piece and sets it on the parapet where the others lay. Ushkar picks it up between finger and thumb and drops it into the pouch at his belt without looking at it. He tips his head at the lantern on its stake. "Light stays. Until you come back over." Then he sits down on the parapet beside his axe, and the conversation is over.

James takes Odo by the elbow. The carter doesn't resist. He seems to have run out of ideas about what he's allowed to do and is grateful to be told. Tamsin steps to James's left without being asked twice, and Pip goes ahead up the ruts with her tail high. At the edge of the lantern light James touches the head of the rod, and a soft glow comes up around the silver coin set there. He tilts it down at the road. The ruts and stones show pale, and Odo's feet stop catching on them.

They're a good stone's throw up the slope before James speaks. Odo answers almost before he's finished, as if he'd been waiting the whole afternoon for someone to ask.

"Not hurt, no. They gave me bread. Bread and a blanket, and the one on the stump kept telling me to stop talking, in that voice, you know, but he never touched me." He breathes. "The salt's Merrow's, sir, but the run's mine. Merrow gave me forty sacks on his chit. Thirty-six gold I owe him for it, when the Arm pays me. And the Arm's buying at forty-eight, for the kitchen. My sister got me the order. Wenna. She's under-cook there. She said they'd always want salt, and I'd have the Arm's custom all winter if I came through on this one." His voice goes thin. "Past the Arm? No. Just the Arm."

The slope gets steeper. Odo shuffles the blanket up onto his shoulder.

"Stopped before? Me, no. Never. I go up the Way to Beregost most years. This road's shorter, and everyone said, you pay the orcs their gold at the bridge and they let you pass, so I thought..." He stops himself. "I saw them on the bridge, and I ran. I don't know why I ran. They caught me before I got to the trees." He doesn't sound angry about it. He sounds embarrassed.

Then he remembers the rest of the question.

"Oh, the notches. That'll be Dannet, likely, among them. Dannet the cooper, three doors down from me in Rivington. They had him in high summer, him and a load of barrels. Three days, and he was home. The Fist paid, every copper of it. He never had to ask. A rider came down from Wyrm's Rock with the coin, and the orcs walked him to the road." Odo nods to himself in the dark. "We all said, well, there's the Fist doing right by us for once. Dannet bought a round on it." He hesitates. "Lost his barrels, mind."

They come round the bent pines, and the light from the rod finds the cart.

It's just as they left it: tipped in the ditch, the canvas lashed tight, the winged stencil showing at the slipped corner. Bess hasn't moved. She lifts her head at the light and makes a low, put-upon sound through her nose, and Odo forgets everything else. He goes to her head and talks into her ear, too low to hear. Pip sniffs once around the wheel and the mule's hooves, finds nothing, and sits down in the ruts to wait. Nobody is at the fat pine.

James works the harness buckles loose one at a time while Odo holds her head. Tamsin swings the pack down and passes him the waterskin. Bess drains it from his cupped hand and the skin's mouth in the time it takes to say so, then shoves her nose against his chest for more.

"She'll want the stream as well, if it's no trouble," Odo says apologetically. "She'll drink half of it."

Under the seat, where a carter keeps what's his, there's a folded brown coat gone shiny at the elbows and a small dented tin box. Odo opens the box under the rod's light to show James there's nothing in it worth an orc's time: two papers. One is Merrow's chit for thirty-six gold, signed with a large untidy M. He doesn't touch the canvas.

Then he turns to James, and in the soft light his face is serious in a way it hasn't been all evening.

"Sorry. I have to ask, or I won't sleep. Seventy gold, sir. I haven't got seventy gold. I won't have it after the Arm pays, either, because the Arm won't pay for salt I haven't brought." He swallows. "How am I meant to pay you back?"

## Player's note — session 1, "The Coast Way"

**What worked**

- **The bridge scene.** It was one long negotiation and it never dragged. Ushkar felt like a real person running a real business: he counts as coins land, has a "different road, different price" logic, takes the bone back so no record goes north, and refuses money for information about the woman. He wasn't a villain and he wasn't a joke. The tone sat right where the world file promised.
- **Hooks that grew from my own choices.** The recut Tymora coin with the eye ties straight to my patron, and the warmth in my own coin made it personal without anyone saying "this is your quest." The Fist paying ransoms fast and quietly through one lieutenant was something I worked out myself from details the DM left lying around: Dannet's story, the "LT" on the bone, the rider with coin. I really liked that the DM never pointed at it.
- **The thing under the bridge.** It's a strong tease. The cat's senses, a flint smell that might just be the lantern, Ushkar's face showing he didn't know about it. It's unexplained, but fair.
- **Rolls only when it mattered.** I asked for Persuasion and the DM declined because the lookout was posted to deliver that answer. That was the right call, and it was explained. DCs were visible, advantage was justified, and the familiar-range rules note asked how my table reads it instead of just ruling.
- **Supporting cast.** Odo's apologies, Tamsin repeating my orders back in fast summary, the mule. The humour came from character, as promised.
- **Costs were real.** 73 gp gone, my waterskin drained, Odo's purse lost, the salt forfeited. Nothing came free.

**What broke or looked off**

- **Clock stuck.** It was full dark with lanterns lit, and the tracker still said "Day 1 · afternoon" the whole session.
- **Money mismatch.** My file says 350 gold. The opening records showed 315 gp, 315 sp and 350 cp, which is 35 gp missing plus silver and copper that came from nowhere. Someone should check how the counters were imported.
- **Rapier inconsistency.** The records say I'm not proficient with martial weapons, but the attack line still shows +5. That should be +2.
- **Truncated text.** Tamsin's party description cuts off mid-sentence ("She").
- **Duplicate note.** One turn had two near-identical out-of-game notes saying "no Persuasion roll."
- **Retroactive patch.** One note added an action after the fact: "I left out his half-step… he did take it." It's minor, but I'd rather the narration just include what I declared.

**What was missing or could be better**

- **Tamsin wasn't reckless.** The brief says she is, but she obeyed every order perfectly and stayed in the gorse. She was charming, but I'd like to see the trait cause trouble: poking at the canvas, mouthing off to an orc, wandering off at the Arm.
- **Some lingering threat.** The talk resolved very cleanly. Ushkar never pushed back on the 70 or tested me, and the lookout's moment of doubt didn't go anywhere. Some leftover tension would make the next session feel like it carries consequences.
- **Corrections in the out-of-game notes.** The lookout's glance and the three-days line were useful, but they read slightly pedantic. One line would do.

Overall it was a very good first session. I left with three threads I care about, a name to send word under, and a door opening at the Friendly Arm. I'd play the next one.

opening.text:
The city is behind you now, only a smudge of smoke to the north. To the west the Sea of Swords has gone the colour of old pewter, and the sun is sliding toward it. Tamsin walks a half-step ahead with your pack hitched high on her shoulders, talking about who on the quay owes whom, and the cat pads along the verge, tail up, stopping now and then to smell the gorse.

Then the road bends around a stand of wind-bent pines, and there is a wagon.

It is a small two-wheeled carter's cart, tipped at an angle, one wheel sunk in the ditch. The mule is still in harness. It lifts its head, looks at you without much interest, and goes back to the grass. Sacks are lashed down under a canvas. Nobody is on the seat, nobody is in the ditch, nobody is on the road as far as you can see, and beyond the bend the road can't be seen at all. Something small and pale lies on the seat, too far away to make out.

Tamsin stops. The cat has stopped too, ears forward, staring at the trees.

"Well," Tamsin says, already shrugging the pack a little lower, "nobody leaves a mule standing. Not on this road." She looks back at you. The light is going. The Friendly Arm is still somewhere ahead.

more.text:
A few things, and most of them are about me rather than the DM.

**The "three days" line was a mistake, not a character choice.** I misjudged the distance to the Gate. When the DM flagged it, I called it James exaggerating to sound put-upon. That was a save after the fact. The DM was right to check.

**The corrections I called pedantic were mostly fixing my errors.** I misread where the lookout looked, and the DM set it straight. I complained about the tone of those notes in my feedback, which isn't quite fair when they kept the fiction straight.

**Tamsin not being reckless is partly my fault.** I said she should cause more trouble, but I gave her an order every single turn: stay left, stay in the gorse, squeeze, don't shout, come down slow. I never left her a gap to be reckless in. The DM played her as someone who'd just been told exactly what to do by a man paying her. Next time I want to give her room and see what she does with it.

**I played it very safe.** Apart from Light, I cast nothing all session. That was mostly right, since nothing called for a fight. But I treated every risk as something to talk around, and that's partly why the scene resolved so cleanly. I asked for "some lingering threat," then took every exit that avoided one.

**I may have made things worse for Odo.** I paid the ransom without bargaining for the salt or the cart. Odo walks away alive but owes Merrow 36 gold, has no cargo, and has lost the Arm's custom. I told him to sort out Merrow himself. In play that felt brisk and soldierly. Now it reads a bit cold. I also just paid into whatever arrangement the Fist has with the bridge, which I suspected even as I counted the coins onto the stone.

**I fished a little.** When I asked whether my coin felt warmer, I was steering the DM toward a patron moment. It paid off, but I also overplayed it with Ushkar ("the same lady") on very little evidence. If that woman turns out to have nothing to do with Tymora, that's on me.

**My out-of-game notes were long.** They often planned three steps ahead or pre-asked for checks. That probably compressed scenes, like the bridge beat where everything happened at once. Shorter declarations would let the DM breathe.

None of this changes my view that it was a good session. I just think a fair note includes my side of the table.
